patient.chief_complaint: Brought in unresponsive after witnessed fall, rhythmic arm movements, history of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease concern — family alarmed by EEG report mentioning 'typical CJD pattern'
patient.hpi: A 67-year-old White female retired teacher was brought to the emergency department by her adult son after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure followed by failure to return to normal consciousness over 90 minutes. She has a 3-month history of rapidly progressive dementia — she went from mild cognitive complaints to being unable to recognize her son and needing full-time care. Her neurologist has been evaluating her for suspected prion disease (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). A brain MRI done 4 weeks ago reportedly showed 'cortical ribboning.' Her neurologist had recently mentioned sporadic CJD was probable per the Paris-Edinburgh criteria. She was not started on any specific treatment (none available for CJD). She takes quetiapine for behavioral symptoms and escitalopram for concurrent depression diagnosed before the dementia. On admission she is unresponsive, making occasional groaning sounds. Her son is very distressed because the previous hospital's EEG was reported as showing 'generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz — typical CJD pattern, highly supportive of prion disease.' The son asks whether the 'seizures' require treatment or whether this is 'just the CJD.' The critical clinical question: are the rhythmic movements true NCSE requiring AED treatment (which could improve quality of life) or are they myoclonic jerks of CJD (which do not respond to AEDs and indicate terminal disease)?

eeg.impression: TWO EEG PATTERNS coexisting: (1) Generalized PSWCs at 1 Hz — typical sporadic CJD pattern; (2) Superimposed left temporal focal ictal runs — suggests true NCSE on the CJD background. This dual pattern is an expert-level diagnostic puzzle. The CJD PSWCs do not require AED treatment. The left temporal NCSE may be treatable. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Glucose 102 mg/dL (H), CSF 14-3-3 protein POSITIVE (strongly positive) qualitative (H), CSF RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) POSITIVE qualitative (H), CSF Total Tau 12840 pg/mL (H).

ct.impression: Diffuse cortical atrophy — consistent with known sCJD. No hemorrhage. MRI previously showed cortical ribboning. CT insufficient for CJD assessment — MRI is the imaging modality of choice.
recommended_actions: MRI brain with DWI/ADC to assess cortical ribboning extent and any focal signal changes
Goals of care discussion with family

output.impression: Extensive bilateral cortical ribboning on DWI with basal ganglia and thalamic involvement — classic advanced sporadic CJD. Left hemisphere slightly more involved than right — correlates with left temporal NCSE on EEG. The focal left temporal NCSE is arising from the most severely affected cortex. Prognosis: median survival sCJD 4-6 months from symptom onset; already 3 months into course. Clinical correlation recommended.
Continue levetiracetam for symptom management. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Quetiapine + escitalopram: both prolong QTc interval via hERG channel blockade. Combination increases risk of QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Given terminal diagnosis and comfort-focused care, obtain ECG and check QTc. If QTc >500 ms, consider reducing or stopping escitalopram. Quetiapine can remain if providing comfort/behavioral benefit.

interactions.description: Levetiracetam has no significant QTc effect — safe to add to quetiapine + escitalopram regimen
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Levetiracetam does not require dose adjustment or cardiac monitoring specific to this combination

output.summary: Quetiapine + escitalopram = QTc prolongation risk. Check ECG. Levetiracetam safe to add. In comfort-focused terminal care, risk-benefit must balance symptom management against QTc risk.

results.title: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: clinical features and management
results.key_finding: sCJD: median survival 4-6 months from symptom onset. EEG PSWCs (generalized periodic sharp waves at 1 Hz) are supportive diagnostic findings. NCSE can complicate terminal sCJD — treat with levetiracetam for comfort management. No disease-modifying treatment exists. RT-QuIC sensitivity >90%, specificity >95% for sCJD. Cortical ribboning on DWI is hallmark imaging finding.

output.summary: sCJD terminal disease: no cure. RT-QuIC is diagnostic. DWI cortical ribboning on MRI is imaging hallmark. EEG PSWCs are typical but do not require AED treatment — CJD PSWCs differ from NCSE. Focal NCSE superimposed on CJD PSWCs: treatable with levetiracetam for comfort.

results.title: Palliative care in prion disease: symptom management and goals of care
results.key_finding: CJD palliative principles: (1) Treat reversible complications (NCSE, infections) if consistent with goals of care; (2) Symptom management priority: myoclonus (clonazepam), agitation (quetiapine/haloperidol), pain/dyspnea; (3) Family support and early hospice referral; (4) Avoid aggressive interventions (ICU, intubation) in terminal disease unless consistent with goals; (5) Confirm advance directive status.

output.summary: sCJD palliative management: treat NCSE with levetiracetam for symptom/comfort; clonazepam for myoclonus; goals of care family meeting early; hospice referral; avoid aggressive interventions unless requested. Confirm advance directive.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) with superimposed focal left temporal NCSE on a background of typical CJD periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) — two separate EEG patterns requiring different treatment approaches

differential.diagnosis: NCSE from autoimmune encephalitis mimicking CJD
differential.key_features: RT-QuIC positive (>95% specificity), 14-3-3 positive, DWI cortical ribboning — these together confirm prion disease; autoimmune antibodies negative
Autoimmune panel negative; RT-QuIC positive; cortical ribboning; PSWCs at 1 Hz are classic sCJD, not autoimmune encephalitis
The KEY insight is that TWO patterns coexist: CJD PSWCs + focal left temporal NCSE; levetiracetam trial confirmed differential response — focal NCSE responds to AED while PSWCs remain unchanged

critical_actions: Distinguish CJD PSWCs from superimposed focal NCSE — AED trial with repeat EEG resolves this
RT-QuIC CSF for sCJD confirmation (>95% specificity)
Goals of care family meeting — terminal disease; NCSE treatment is comfort-focused
Check QTc — quetiapine + escitalopram combination carries QTc prolongation risk
Do NOT use succinylcholine, Do NOT intubate without goals-of-care discussion in terminal patient
contraindicated_actions: Aggressive AED escalation targeting CJD PSWCs — these do not respond to AEDs and represent the CJD process itself
Intubation and ICU admission without goals-of-care discussion — terminal disease; aggressive interventions require explicit family consent
Diagnosing all rhythmic movements as CJD without EEG — superimposed NCSE in terminal disease is treatable for comfort
key_reasoning_points: Expert-level distinction: CJD PSWCs and focal NCSE coexist on the same EEG — differential AED response (focal NCSE reduces while PSWCs remain) proves two separate patterns
RT-QuIC has >95% specificity for prion disease — positive result is essentially diagnostic in the appropriate clinical context
CJD PSWCs at 1 Hz are a diagnostic criterion for sCJD — they represent the prion disease process, NOT treatable NCSE; do not escalate AEDs targeting PSWCs
Focal NCSE superimposed on CJD represents a treatable complication worth addressing for quality of life and family comfort (patient appears less distressed)
QTc risk: quetiapine + escitalopram both prolong QTc; levetiracetam is safe to add; monitor ECG in terminal patients receiving these agents

red_herrings.data_point: EEG report: 'generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz — typical CJD pattern'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude ALL rhythmic EEG activity is CJD and no AED treatment is needed
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CJD PSWCs are present, but additional left focal ictal activity is a SEPARATE pattern representing superimposed NCSE. AED trial with repeat EEG reveals differential response. Both diagnoses coexist.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Decide no treatment is appropriate for any EEG abnormality
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Terminal disease does not mean no treatment. Superimposed NCSE causes additional suffering and reduced awareness — levetiracetam can improve quality of remaining life consistent with comfort-focused goals.

metadata.teaching_points: sCJD PSWCs vs superimposed NCSE; RT-QuIC diagnostic specificity; differential AED response distinguishes two EEG patterns; goals of care in terminal disease; QTc risk with quetiapine + SSRI
metadata.pitfalls: Treating all rhythmic activity as CJD without EEG; aggressive treatment without goals-of-care discussion; missing QTc prolongation from quetiapine + SSRI
metadata.clinical_pearl: sCJD + focal EEG seizure activity: perform AED trial. CJD PSWCs do not respond. Focal NCSE does respond. Both can coexist. RT-QuIC is >95% specific for prion disease. Goals of care first in terminal disease.
